course.title: Architecture: A Visual History
course.description: A guided walk through five thousand years of building, from the stone temples of Egypt to the rippling steel of today, teaching you to read any structure by its form, function, materials, and the way it carries its load. Structure and examples adapted from the History of architecture entry on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Each lesson pairs a clear idea with real, famous buildings you can picture.

questions.prompt: The oldest way to span an opening is the post-and-lintel: two uprights carrying a horizontal beam. The horizontal piece is the…
questions.explanation: The upright 'posts' carry a 'lintel' across the gap. You see it in Stonehenge and in every Greek temple porch.

questions.prompt: When a stone column holds up the weight of a roof, the force squeezing down through the column is called…
questions.explanation: Stone and brick are strong in compression (being squeezed) but weak in tension (being pulled), which shapes how they can be built.

questions.prompt: The three classical orders of ancient Greek architecture are Doric, Ionic, and…
questions.explanation: Doric is plain, Ionic has scroll-shaped volutes, and Corinthian is topped with carved acanthus leaves. The Romans later added Tuscan and Composite.

questions.prompt: The Roman innovation that let builders span wide openings with small wedge-shaped stones, each pushing against its neighbors, is the…
questions.explanation: In a round arch the wedge stones (voussoirs) lock together in compression, carrying far wider spans than a single stone lintel ever could.

questions.prompt: Rotate a round arch in a full circle around its center and you enclose a space with a…
questions.explanation: A dome is, in effect, an arch spun around a vertical axis. Rome's Pantheon is the great early example.

questions.prompt: The pointed arch, the ribbed vault, and the flying buttress are the signature features of which style?
questions.explanation: Gothic builders used these three devices together to raise thin, tall walls pierced by huge stained-glass windows, as at Chartres and Notre-Dame de Paris.

questions.prompt: The phrase 'form follows function', a slogan of modern architecture, was coined by…
questions.explanation: The American architect Louis Sullivan wrote it in 1896; it became a rallying cry for designing a building around its purpose rather than past styles.

questions.prompt: A material is especially associated with Roman engineering because it could be poured into molds and set underwater. It is…
questions.explanation: Roman concrete (opus caementicium), made with volcanic ash, let them cast the Pantheon's dome and vast vaulted halls in one monolithic shell.

lessons.title: How to read a building
lessons.grammar_note: Load is the weight and force a building must carry; support is the path of columns, walls, and foundations that carries it safely to the ground. Every structure is a conversation between the two.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to look at almost any building and break it down into four plain questions: what is its form, what is its function, how is it built, and what is it made of. You will also be able to tell load from support, which is the single idea that unlocks the whole history ahead. Warm-up from the diagnostic: in a post-and-lintel gate, which piece is being squeezed in compression and which is bending across the gap? Hold that picture, because every arch, vault, and steel frame to come is just a cleverer answer to the same problem: how to get weight safely down to the ground. Reading a building is a skill, not a talent, and the four questions are your toolkit.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Start with four lenses. Form is the building's shape and appearance: its outline, proportions, and ornament. Function is its purpose: a temple, a market, a home, an office. Structure is the system that keeps it standing. Materials are what it is made from: stone, brick, timber, concrete, iron, glass, steel. Now the physics. Every building carries loads. The dead load is the weight of the building itself; the live load is people, furniture, and snow; lateral loads are sideways pushes from wind and earthquakes. These forces must travel along a continuous path of support, through beams, columns, and walls, down into the foundation and the earth. Two kinds of force matter most. Compression squeezes a material together, and tension stretches it apart. Stone and brick resist compression well but crack under tension, which is why ancient builders favored columns, arches, and domes that keep everything in compression. Later, iron and steel, strong in tension too, would change what shapes were possible.

sections.heading: Key works & builders
sections.text: Picture three buildings as a crash course. Stonehenge, raised in prehistoric Britain, is pure post-and-lintel: upright stones carrying horizontal ones, the simplest way to make a doorway, limited by how far a single beam can span before it snaps. The Parthenon in Athens is the same system perfected in marble, its columns in compression holding a roof of stone and timber. Jump forward and the Crystal Palace, built in London in 1851 from prefabricated iron and glass, carries its loads through a slender metal skeleton instead of heavy walls, letting light pour in. Three buildings, three answers to one question. As you study each era, keep asking the same things: where does the weight go, what spans the openings, and what material made that span possible. The names and dates matter less than the logic of load and support running underneath them all.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) In a post-and-lintel doorway, which member is most likely to crack from bending? 2) Name the dead load and a live load for a library reading room. 3) Why could ancient builders not make a stone lintel span a very wide gap? 4) Which two forces are compression and tension, and which one does plain stone resist well? 5) What are the four lenses for reading a building? Answers: 1) The lintel, which bends across the gap and feels tension on its underside. 2) Dead load: the weight of the shelves, floors, and roof; live load: the readers, chairs, and books. 3) Stone is weak in tension, so a long lintel cracks under its own bending. 4) Compression squeezes, tension stretches; stone resists compression well. 5) Form, function, structure, and materials.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a building's style is just decoration. Ornament matters, but structure and materials usually drive the shape; the pointed arch and the glass skyscraper exist because of how they carry load, not because they look nice. Mistake: assuming thicker always means stronger. A slender steel frame can outperform a massive stone wall, because the material, not the bulk, decides what is possible. Mistake: forgetting lateral loads; many failures come from sideways wind or earthquake forces, not from gravity alone. Exit ticket: (a) What path must every load follow to be safe? (b) Which force stretches a material, and which building material is poor at resisting it? Answers: every load travels through beams, columns, and walls into the foundation and the ground; tension stretches, and stone (or brick) is poor at resisting it.

lessons.title: Ancient architecture: Egypt, Greece, and Rome
lessons.grammar_note: A barrel vault is a continuous arch forming a tunnel; a groin vault is two barrel vaults crossing at right angles; a dome is an arch rotated around a center. All three are ways of roofing space without a flat beam.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to trace a clear line from the solid stone of Egypt, through the refined columns of Greece, to the arches, vaults, domes, and concrete of Rome, and to say what each civilization added to the toolkit of building. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you already named the three Greek orders and the Roman arch. In this lesson you will see why the arch was such a leap. Egypt and Greece built mostly with post-and-lintel, so their interiors were forests of closely spaced columns, because stone beams cannot reach far. Rome broke that limit with the arch and its relatives, opening up wide, uninterrupted halls. Keep the load-and-support question from last lesson in mind; this whole lesson is Rome learning to put masonry in pure compression over ever larger spans.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Egyptian architecture is massive, permanent, and built for the gods and the dead. Using post-and-lintel in enormous blocks, Egyptians raised the pyramids at Giza and temple halls crowded with thick columns, because stone lintels can only span a short distance. Greek architecture refined the column into a system of three orders: the plain Doric, the scroll-topped Ionic, and the leafy Corinthian. Greek temples added subtle visual corrections, such as entasis, a slight swelling of the column so it does not look pinched. But Greece, too, was bound by the short stone beam. Rome changed everything with three devices in compression: the round arch, built from wedge-shaped voussoirs; the vault, an arch extended into a tunnel (barrel) or crossed (groin); and the dome, an arch spun full circle. Rome also perfected concrete made with volcanic ash, which could be poured into molds, set even underwater, and faced with brick or stone. Together these let Romans roof vast spaces no Greek could.

sections.heading: Key works & builders
sections.text: In Egypt, the Great Pyramid of Giza and the hypostyle hall at Karnak, with its thicket of giant columns, show post-and-lintel at monumental scale. In Greece, the Parthenon on the Athenian Acropolis is the Doric order at its most refined, while the Erechtheion nearby shows the Ionic order and its famous carved maidens, the caryatids. In Rome, the Colosseum stacks arcades of arches in the three orders to seat tens of thousands; the Pont du Gard aqueduct in France carries water across a valley on tiers of arches; and the Pantheon crowns a cylindrical hall with an unreinforced concrete dome over forty meters across, lit by a single round opening, the oculus, at its top. The Pantheon's dome stood as the largest in the world for more than a thousand years, a direct result of Roman concrete and the geometry of the arch turned in a circle.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) Why were Egyptian and Greek interiors so full of columns? 2) Which Greek order is topped with acanthus leaves? 3) What are the wedge-shaped stones of an arch called? 4) Name the two vault types and how they differ. 5) What ingredient made Roman concrete so durable, and name the building it crowns most famously. Answers: 1) They used post-and-lintel, and stone beams can only span short distances, so columns had to be close together. 2) The Corinthian order. 3) Voussoirs. 4) A barrel vault is a single arch extended into a tunnel; a groin vault is two barrel vaults crossing at right angles. 5) Volcanic ash; it is cast into the dome of the Pantheon.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling every ancient temple 'Roman'. If the building is columns and straight beams with no arches, it is closer to the Greek or Egyptian tradition; arches, vaults, and domes point to Rome. Mistake: thinking the Greeks built arches freely. They knew the arch but rarely used it for show; the arch became a defining Roman tool. Mistake: picturing the Pantheon's dome as stone blocks. It is largely concrete, lighter aggregate near the top, which is why it could span so far. Exit ticket: (a) What single device let Rome roof far wider spaces than Greece could? (b) What is the opening at the top of the Pantheon's dome called? Answers: the arch (and its vaults and domes), worked in concrete; the opening is the oculus.

lessons.title: Byzantine and Islamic architecture
lessons.grammar_note: A pendentive is the curved triangular piece that lets a round dome sit on a square room, carrying the dome's weight down to four corner piers. It is the key to putting a circle on a square.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to explain how Byzantine builders solved the problem of setting a round dome over a square room, and how Islamic architecture turned the arch, the dome, and pure geometry into a new language of light and ornament. Warm-up from the last lesson: Rome gave you the dome, but a Roman dome usually sat on a round drum, like the Pantheon. What happens when you want that dome over a square hall, which is far more useful for a building with four walls? The answer, the pendentive, is a small triangle of masonry with enormous consequences, and it opens the whole eastern tradition. Keep tracing load to the ground; this lesson is really about gathering a dome's weight onto four points.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: When the Roman Empire's center shifted east to Constantinople, Byzantine architecture grew around the domed church. Its signature solution is the pendentive: four curved triangles rising from the corners of a square to form a continuous circular ring on which a dome can rest. The weight of the dome is funneled through the pendentives down to four massive piers, freeing the walls below to open up. Interiors glow with gold mosaics and are flooded with light from windows ringing the dome's base. Islamic architecture, spreading from the seventh century across a vast region, drew on both Roman and Byzantine ideas and developed its own forms: the pointed and horseshoe arch, the central dome, slender towers called minarets, and the courtyard. Because figural images were generally avoided in religious settings, decoration turned to intricate geometric patterns, flowing plant forms (arabesques), and calligraphy, along with muqarnas, the honeycomb-like clusters of small niches that soften the join between wall and dome.

sections.heading: Key works & builders
sections.text: The masterpiece of Byzantine building is the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople (modern Istanbul), completed in 537 for the emperor Justinian by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus. Its huge central dome seems to float, because a ring of windows at its base makes the supporting masonry almost disappear. In the Islamic world, the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (691) is among the earliest great monuments; the Great Mosque of Cordoba in Spain dazzles with rows of striped double arches multiplying into the distance; and the Alhambra palace in Granada layers courtyards, reflecting pools, and ceilings dripping with muqarnas. Later, the Mughal dynasty in India produced the Taj Mahal (completed around 1653), a white marble tomb whose swelling central dome, framing arches, and perfect symmetry show how far the tradition traveled. Across all of these, notice the shared logic: a dome gathered onto a few strong points, walls opened to light, and surfaces alive with geometry rather than statues.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) What problem does a pendentive solve? 2) Where does a pendentive send the dome's weight? 3) Name two features typical of Islamic religious architecture. 4) Why did Islamic decoration favor geometry, plants, and calligraphy? 5) Name the Byzantine building whose dome appears to float, and say why it seems to. Answers: 1) It lets a round dome sit over a square room. 2) Down to four corner piers. 3) Any two of: pointed or horseshoe arches, central dome, minarets, courtyards, muqarnas. 4) Figural images were generally avoided in religious settings, so artists developed non-figural ornament. 5) The Hagia Sophia; a ring of windows at the dome's base hides its supports, so the dome looks suspended.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing a pendentive with a squinch. Both bridge from square to circle, but a pendentive is a continuous curved triangle, while a squinch is a small arch or lintel laid across each corner; Byzantine domes made the pendentive famous. Mistake: treating Islamic architecture as a single style. It spans many centuries and regions, from Spain to India, with strong local differences. Mistake: thinking the Hagia Sophia was always a mosque; it began as a Byzantine church, later became a mosque, and its history reflects the city's. Exit ticket: (a) What curved triangle lets a dome sit on a square? (b) What are the honeycomb-like niches in Islamic ceilings called? Answers: the pendentive; muqarnas.

questions.prompt: The two forces that matter most in masonry are compression and tension. Plain stone is strong in…
questions.explanation: Stone resists squeezing (compression) well but cracks when stretched (tension), which is why ancient builders used columns, arches, and domes.

questions.prompt: Egyptian and early Greek interiors were crowded with columns because they relied on…
questions.explanation: A stone lintel can only span a short distance, so the columns had to be placed close together.

questions.prompt: The three classical Greek orders, from plainest to most ornate, are…
questions.explanation: Doric is plainest, Ionic has scroll volutes, and Corinthian is the leafiest, topped with carved acanthus.

questions.prompt: Roman concrete, the arch, and the vault together allowed Rome to…
options: roof far wider spaces than Greece could
questions.explanation: Arches, vaults, and poured concrete carried loads in compression over large spans, giving Rome vast open interiors like the Pantheon.

options: set a round dome over a square room
questions.explanation: The curved triangular pendentives carry a circular dome down onto four piers at the corners of a square, as in the Hagia Sophia.

questions.prompt: Islamic religious decoration relied mainly on geometry, plant forms, and calligraphy because…
questions.explanation: With figural imagery generally avoided in religious settings, artists developed rich non-figural ornament, including muqarnas and arabesques.

lessons.title: Romanesque and Gothic: the age of cathedrals
lessons.grammar_note: A flying buttress is an external half-arch that catches the sideways thrust of a vault and carries it down to a freestanding pier outside the building, so the inner wall can be thin and full of windows.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to tell a Romanesque church from a Gothic one at a glance, and explain the three devices, the pointed arch, the ribbed vault, and the flying buttress, that let Gothic builders raise walls of stone and glass toward the sky. Warm-up from the last lesson: you know how a dome's thrust is gathered onto piers. A barrel vault has a similar problem, it pushes outward along its whole length, so the walls holding it must be thick and heavy. Romanesque builders accepted those heavy walls; Gothic builders found a way around them. This lesson is the story of walls getting thinner, windows getting bigger, and interiors getting taller and brighter, all driven by better ways to handle the outward thrust of a vault.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Romanesque architecture, flourishing across Europe around the eleventh and twelfth centuries, is built from round arches and heavy barrel or groin vaults. Because those vaults push outward, the walls must be thick and the windows small, giving Romanesque interiors a solid, dim, fortress-like feel. Gothic architecture, emerging in France in the twelfth century, solved the thrust problem with three linked ideas. The pointed arch directs more of its load straight downward rather than outward, so it needs less buttressing and can be made taller or wider at will. The ribbed vault concentrates the roof's weight onto slender ribs that meet at a few points, instead of pressing along a whole wall. And the flying buttress reaches out from the building to catch the remaining outward thrust and carry it down to piers set clear of the wall. Freed from carrying the vault, the walls between could melt away into tall windows filled with stained glass, flooding the interior with colored light.

sections.heading: Key works & builders
sections.text: For Romanesque, Durham Cathedral in England shows massive piers and some of the earliest ribbed vaulting, while the Speyer Cathedral in Germany and the Leaning Tower of Pisa (part of a Romanesque complex) show the round-arched, heavy-walled style. The Gothic revolution is often traced to the choir of the Abbey of Saint-Denis near Paris, rebuilt under Abbot Suger around 1140 to let in light as a spiritual idea. The great French cathedrals followed: Notre-Dame de Paris, with early flying buttresses; Chartres, famous for its blue stained glass; and Reims and Amiens, soaring ever higher. In England, Salisbury Cathedral shows the style's reach. These buildings were the work of master masons and whole towns over generations, not single architects, and they competed to build taller and brighter, pushing stone construction to its very limit before iron arrived.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) Why are Romanesque walls so thick and their windows so small? 2) How does a pointed arch help compared with a round one? 3) What does a ribbed vault concentrate, and onto what? 4) What does a flying buttress do with the vault's outward thrust? 5) Name a Gothic cathedral and one feature it is known for. Answers: 1) Their round-arched barrel and groin vaults push outward, so thick walls are needed to resist the thrust, leaving little room for windows. 2) A pointed arch directs more load straight down and less outward, so it needs less buttressing and can go taller. 3) It concentrates the roof's weight onto slender ribs meeting at a few points. 4) It catches the outward thrust and carries it down to a freestanding pier outside the wall. 5) For example, Chartres, known for its stained glass, or Notre-Dame de Paris for its flying buttresses.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking flying buttresses are just decoration. They are working structure, catching the vault's outward push so the walls can be thin; remove them and tall Gothic walls would lean out and fall. Mistake: assuming pointed arches are only about looks. Their shape is structural, redirecting load downward. Mistake: calling any old, heavy church 'Gothic'. If it has round arches, thick walls, and small windows, it is Romanesque; pointed arches, big stained glass, and flying buttresses mark the Gothic. Exit ticket: (a) Which three devices define Gothic construction? (b) What did thinning the walls allow builders to fill them with? Answers: the pointed arch, the ribbed vault, and the flying buttress; large windows of stained glass.

lessons.title: The Renaissance and the Baroque
lessons.grammar_note: Renaissance means 'rebirth'; in architecture it is the deliberate revival of ancient Greek and Roman forms, governed by symmetry, clear proportion, and the classical orders. The Baroque keeps those forms but bends them into drama and movement.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to describe how Renaissance architects revived the calm, ordered classical language after the Gothic age, and how Baroque architects then charged that same language with drama, curves, and motion. Warm-up from the last lesson: Gothic cathedrals reached upward with pointed arches and soaring height. The Renaissance deliberately turned back to the round arches, columns, and domes of Rome, prizing balance and human-scaled proportion over Gothic verticality. Keep the structural thread too: one of the era's defining feats was a dome so large that builders had to rediscover and reinvent how to raise it at all. This lesson pairs two linked styles, one about order and one about drama, and introduces architects we can name as individuals, a shift from the anonymous masons of the cathedrals.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Renaissance architecture, beginning in fifteenth-century Italy, revived the vocabulary of ancient Rome: the round arch, the classical orders, the dome, and above all symmetry and mathematical proportion. Buildings were composed as balanced, legible wholes, often centered on a clear geometric plan. Architecture became a learned art, and designers began to publish treatises and sign their work. The Baroque, from the late sixteenth century onward, used the same classical elements but set them in motion. Facades curve in and out, walls ripple, spaces swell into ovals, and light is staged for emotional effect, often in the service of a grand church or an absolute monarch. Where a Renaissance building invites calm contemplation of its proportions, a Baroque building sweeps you along. Both styles depend on the orders and the arch you already know; the difference is attitude. Renaissance: ordered, serene, balanced. Baroque: dynamic, theatrical, overwhelming. Understanding one makes the other easy to read.

sections.heading: Key works & builders
sections.text: The Renaissance opens with Filippo Brunelleschi, who roofed the crossing of Florence Cathedral (Santa Maria del Fiore) with an enormous brick dome completed in 1436, engineering a double-shell structure and a herringbone brick pattern to raise it without a full timber framework. Leon Battista Alberti wrote influential treatises, and Donato Bramante designed the jewel-like Tempietto in Rome. Andrea Palladio, working around Venice, built the perfectly symmetrical Villa Rotonda and published 'The Four Books of Architecture', whose rules shaped country houses for centuries, even reaching American buildings like Monticello. For the Baroque, Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed the sweeping oval colonnade embracing St. Peter's Square in Rome, while his rival Francesco Borromini bent walls into restless curves at San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane. The Palace of Versailles in France shows the Baroque enlisted for royal spectacle. Together these names mark the moment the architect steps forward as a celebrated individual artist.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) What ancient tradition did Renaissance architecture revive? 2) Name the two qualities Renaissance design prized most. 3) How does a Baroque building differ in feeling from a Renaissance one? 4) Who built the great dome of Florence Cathedral, and roughly when? 5) Which Renaissance architect wrote 'The Four Books of Architecture' and designed the Villa Rotonda? Answers: 1) The classical architecture of ancient Greece and Rome. 2) Symmetry and clear mathematical proportion (balance and order). 3) A Baroque building is dynamic, curved, and theatrical, staging light and movement, where a Renaissance building is calm and balanced. 4) Filippo Brunelleschi, completed in 1436. 5) Andrea Palladio.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the Renaissance invented new structural forms. Its genius was revival and refinement of Roman forms, plus feats of engineering like Brunelleschi's dome, not a brand-new structural system. Mistake: treating Baroque as merely 'fancy Renaissance'. The difference is a deliberate shift toward movement, curve, and drama, not just more ornament. Mistake: assuming symmetry means dullness; Renaissance symmetry was a sophisticated pursuit of harmony and human proportion. Exit ticket: (a) In one word each, how would you describe the mood of Renaissance versus Baroque architecture? (b) Name the engineering challenge Brunelleschi is famous for solving. Answers: Renaissance is ordered (or serene), Baroque is dynamic (or dramatic); he raised the vast dome of Florence Cathedral without a conventional full timber framework, using a double shell and herringbone brickwork.

lessons.title: The industrial era: iron, glass, and the skyscraper
lessons.grammar_note: A steel frame (or skeleton frame) is a grid of vertical columns and horizontal beams that carries the whole weight of a building, so the outer walls become a light 'curtain' that hangs on the frame instead of holding the building up.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to explain how new industrial materials, cast iron, wrought iron, plate glass, and then steel, broke the limits of stone and brick and made possible two new building types: the vast glass-and-iron hall and the skyscraper. Warm-up from earlier lessons: for thousands of years, height and span were limited because stone and brick are weak in tension and heavy. The industrial revolution introduced materials that are strong in tension and can be mass-produced to exact sizes in a factory. Keep the load path in mind, because the big idea here is moving the load off the walls and onto a slender internal frame, so the walls no longer have to hold the building up. That single shift is what lets a building grow taller than ever before and open its skin to light.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The nineteenth century brought iron and then steel into building at scale. Iron is strong in both compression and tension and can be cast or rolled into precise, repeatable parts, so structures could be prefabricated and bolted together quickly. Combined with large sheets of plate glass, iron produced a new architecture of light: train sheds, exhibition halls, arcades, and conservatories enclosing huge spaces with slender frames and glazed roofs. The second revolution was vertical. By framing a building with a steel skeleton, the frame, not the walls, carries all the loads. The exterior wall becomes a thin curtain wall, often mostly glass, hung on the frame. Add the safety elevator, which made upper floors usable, and reliable steel, and the skyscraper is born: a tall building whose height is limited by economics and engineering rather than by the strength of a masonry wall. Reinforced concrete, concrete cast around steel bars to give it tensile strength, became the other great modern material, versatile and fireproof.

sections.heading: Key works & builders
sections.text: The era's early emblem is the Crystal Palace, designed by Joseph Paxton for London's Great Exhibition of 1851, a colossal building of prefabricated iron and glass assembled in months. In Paris, the Eiffel Tower of 1889, engineered by Gustave Eiffel, showed wrought iron reaching heights no masonry tower could. Grand railway stations roofed their platforms with sweeping iron-and-glass vaults. The skyscraper grew up in the United States: the Home Insurance Building in Chicago (1885), by William Le Baron Jenney, is often called the first tall building carried by a metal skeleton frame. The Chicago School and the architect Louis Sullivan shaped the early tall office building and its ornament, and Sullivan's phrase 'form follows function' pointed toward the century ahead. In New York, the Flatiron Building (1902) made the steel-framed tower a symbol of the modern city. Behind all of them stands the same quiet revolution: the frame carries the weight, so the wall can be glass.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) Why could iron do things stone and brick could not? 2) In a steel-frame building, what carries the loads, and what becomes of the outer wall? 3) What two inventions, besides the steel frame, made the skyscraper practical? 4) What is reinforced concrete, and why is the steel in it important? 5) Name an early iron-and-glass building and an early steel-framed skyscraper. Answers: 1) Iron is strong in both compression and tension and can be mass-produced in exact, repeatable parts, unlike heavy, tension-weak stone. 2) The steel skeleton frame carries the loads; the outer wall becomes a light curtain wall, often glass. 3) The safety elevator and reliable mass-produced steel (plus, broadly, better foundations). 4) Concrete cast around steel bars; the steel gives the concrete the tensile strength it otherwise lacks. 5) Iron-and-glass: the Crystal Palace; steel-framed skyscraper: the Home Insurance Building in Chicago.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a skyscraper's stone or glass skin holds it up. In a framed building the skin is a curtain hung on the steel; the frame does the work. Mistake: crediting a single person with 'inventing' the skyscraper. It emerged from many advances, the elevator, cheap steel, the frame, fireproofing, and foundations, coming together in 1880s Chicago. Mistake: assuming concrete is weak. Plain concrete is weak in tension, but reinforced with steel bars it becomes one of the strongest and most versatile building materials. Exit ticket: (a) What does a steel frame let the outer wall become? (b) Which Chicago building is often called the first skeleton-framed skyscraper? Answers: a light, non-loadbearing curtain wall, often of glass; the Home Insurance Building (1885).

items.translation: two uprights (posts) carrying a horizontal beam (lintel); the oldest way to span an opening
items.example: Stonehenge and the Greek temple porch are both post-and-lintel construction.

items.translation: one of the wedge-shaped stones that make up an arch, locking together in compression
items.example: The topmost voussoir of an arch is the keystone.

items.translation: an arched structure of masonry forming a ceiling; a barrel vault is a tunnel, a groin vault is two barrels crossed
items.example: Romanesque churches are roofed with heavy barrel vaults.

items.translation: a curved triangular element that lets a round dome rest over a square room by carrying its weight to four piers
items.example: The pendentives of the Hagia Sophia make its dome seem to float.

items.translation: an external half-arch that carries a vault's outward thrust to a freestanding pier, letting the wall be thin
items.example: Flying buttresses let Gothic cathedrals open their walls into stained glass.

items.translation: a system of designing a column and what it carries; the Greek orders are Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian
items.example: The Corinthian order is recognized by its carved acanthus leaves.

items.translation: a non-loadbearing outer wall, often glass, that hangs on a building's frame rather than supporting it
items.example: A steel-framed skyscraper wears a glass curtain wall.

items.translation: a beam or slab fixed at one end only, projecting into space with no support under its far end
items.example: The dramatic terraces of Fallingwater are cantilevered over the stream.

lessons.title: Modernism and contemporary architecture
lessons.grammar_note: 'Form follows function' (Louis Sullivan, 1896) means a building's shape should grow from its purpose, not from borrowed historical styles. Modernism took this as a creed; later architects would argue back against it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to describe the modern movement, its stripped-down glass-and-steel buildings and its slogan 'form follows function', and then trace what came after it: the playful return of ornament in postmodernism, the sculptural curves of today's star architects, and the rise of sustainable, green design. Warm-up from the last lesson: the steel frame and reinforced concrete freed the wall from carrying load. Modern architects embraced that freedom to strip buildings down to clean lines, open plans, and glass skins, rejecting the historical styles of the past. This final lesson runs from roughly 1920 to today, so keep asking your four questions, form, function, structure, materials, as the answers grow bolder and the shapes, thanks to computers and new engineering, grow freer than ever.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Modernism, taking shape in the 1920s, rejected historical ornament and sought a new architecture honest to industrial materials: steel, concrete, and glass. Its ideals were clean geometry, open flowing interiors, flat roofs, large windows, and the belief that a building's form should follow its function. The German Bauhaus school fused art, craft, and industry; the International Style spread flat-roofed, white, unornamented buildings worldwide. After the Second World War, glass-and-steel towers with curtain walls became the face of the modern city. From the 1960s and 70s, reactions set in. Postmodernism argued that pure modernism was cold and dull, and brought back color, ornament, history, and wit. High-tech architecture celebrated the structure and services by putting them on the outside. More recently, powerful computers and new engineering have let architects build sweeping, sculptural curves once impossible to draw or construct. Running through the latest work is sustainable or green design: orienting, insulating, and shading a building to use far less energy, and choosing materials for their environmental cost.

sections.heading: Key works & builders
sections.text: Modernism's giants include Walter Gropius, who founded the Bauhaus; Le Corbusier, whose Villa Savoye near Paris demonstrates his 'five points' (including pilotis, the slim columns lifting the house, and a free facade) and who called a house 'a machine for living in'; Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, whose motto 'less is more' produced the pristine Barcelona Pavilion and the Seagram Building in New York; and Frank Lloyd Wright, whose Fallingwater cantilevers its terraces over a waterfall. Louis Sullivan's 'form follows function' underpins it all. For the reaction, Robert Venturi answered 'less is a bore', and Michael Graves's colorful Portland Building and Philip Johnson's AT&T Building (now 550 Madison) announced postmodernism; the Pompidou Centre in Paris, by Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers, turned a building inside out. Today Frank Gehry's titanium-clad Guggenheim Museum Bilbao and Zaha Hadid's flowing Heydar Aliyev Center show architecture as sculpture, while buildings like Milan's plant-covered Bosco Verticale carry the banner of green design.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) What did modernism reject, and what three materials did it celebrate? 2) Who coined 'form follows function', and who answered 'less is a bore'? 3) What did postmodernism bring back that modernism had stripped away? 4) What makes today's sweeping, curved buildings buildable now? 5) What is the central aim of sustainable, or green, design, and name a building known for it. Answers: 1) It rejected historical ornament; it celebrated steel, concrete, and glass. 2) Louis Sullivan coined 'form follows function'; Robert Venturi answered 'less is a bore'. 3) Color, ornament, historical references, and wit. 4) Powerful computer modeling and new engineering and fabrication methods. 5) To cut a building's energy use and environmental impact through orientation, insulation, shading, and material choices; for example, the Bosco Verticale in Milan.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking 'modern' just means 'recent'. Modernism is a specific movement with specific ideals, clean lines, honest materials, form following function, not simply any new building. Mistake: reading 'less is more' and 'less is a bore' as the same debate about taste; they mark a real shift from modernist restraint to postmodern play. Mistake: treating green design as mere add-on technology. The most effective sustainability is passive, built into a building's shape, orientation, and materials from the start. Exit ticket: (a) Which slogan sums up the modern movement, and who said it? (b) Name one architect celebrated for sculptural, curving contemporary buildings. Answers: 'form follows function', by Louis Sullivan; for example, Frank Gehry or Zaha Hadid.
